stops.name: Molay, the village in the County of Burgundy
stops.campa: In the wooded march of the Franche-Comté, under the Empire and not the crown of France, a son is born to the minor nobility at Molay. The land is poor, the winters hard, the horizon closed by the ridges of the Amont. He grows a boy of the frontier, hearing at Mass and market of the far kingdom across the sea, of Jerusalem lost and won and lost again, of the white mantle with the red cross that a man may earn if he give up all he has. The call is already in the air of the country before he knows his own name for it.

stops.name: Beaune, the reception in the chapel of the Temple
stops.campa: By night, in the chapel of the Temple house at Beaune, Jacques is received into the Order of the Poor Knights of Christ. Humbert de Pairaud, Visitor of France and England, receives him; Amaury de la Roche, Master of France, stands by. He kneels, asks the bread and water of the house and the company of the brethren, and swears the threefold vow: poverty, chastity, obedience. They lay the white mantle with its red cross upon his shoulders and give him the kiss of peace. From this night he owns nothing; he is a soldier of God and the Temple until death.
stops.quote: I was received at Beaune, in the diocese of Autun, by Brother Humbert de Pairaud, in the presence of Brother Amaury de la Roche and others.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jacques de Molay, papal inquest (as recorded in the trial proceedings)

stops.name: Acre, the Templar quarter in the last capital of the Kingdom
stops.campa: Molay crosses the sea to Outremer, to Acre, the last great city of the Christian East, where the Temple holds its strongest house behind the sea wall at the western tip. The kingdom of Jerusalem is a kingdom without Jerusalem now: a strip of coast, a scatter of castles, a truce always breaking. He serves in the ranks of the white knights through twenty years the chronicles scarcely record: garrison, patrol, the long dwindling of the Frankish East as Baibars and then Qalawun take the inland fortresses one by one. He learns the Order as a fighting brotherhood in its own last country.

stops.name: Château Pèlerin (Atlit), the great sea-castle of the Temple
stops.campa: South of Acre the Temple holds its mightiest fortress, Château Pèlerin (Atlit, the Pilgrim's Castle), thrust into the sea on its own headland, walls the Saracen never storms. Here and at Sidon, at Tortosa and Beirut, the white knights keep the shrinking coast. Molay comes up through the Order's inner councils in these years, a man of the frontier who has seen from a rampart the whole Frankish East pared back to a rind of shore. When Acre falls, Atlit will hold a few weeks more, then be abandoned to the waves, the last castle given up without a siege.

stops.name: Acre, the walls breached, the Gate of Saint Anthony
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of May the Mamluk host of al-Ashraf Khalil pours through the breached Accursed Tower. Grand Master Guillaume de Beaujeu, roused from sleep, gathers his knights and rides into the storm at the Gate of Saint Anthony. An arrow finds the gap in his mail beneath the raised arm; his men cry that he flees, and turning he shows them the shaft. 'I am not fleeing,' he answers, 'I am dead. See the blow.' They bear him back to die within the Temple. The city is lost; the streets run with the fall of two hundred years of the Christian kingdom of the East.
stops.quote: I am not fleeing; I am dead. Behold the blow.
stops.quote_source: The 'Templar of Tyre' (Gestes des Chiprois), on the death of Guillaume de Beaujeu

stops.name: Acre, the last stand of the Temple by the sea, the flight to the ships
stops.campa: The city falls, but the seaward Temple fortress with its four towers holds days more, crowded with knights and thousands of the terrified. Marshal Peter de Sevrey commands the last stand. Offered safe passage, he sends the women and children to the galleys; when the Mamluks break faith and lay hands on them, the brothers shut the gates and fight. Sevrey, going out under truce to the Sultan's tent, is beheaded. On the twenty-eighth the undermined wall collapses; the Saracens rush the breach and the last Templars die in the ruin. Small boats pull for Cyprus over a red harbour. Outremer is finished.

stops.name: Sidon, the sea-castle abandoned, the coast given up
stops.campa: In the weeks after Acre the whole Latin shore falls without a fight. The Templars hold Sidon a little while (the sea-castle on its causeway, the last refuge of the Marshal and the Grand Master's own household), then, hopeless of relief, put out for Cyprus and leave it to the Mamluk. Tortosa and Atlit follow before summer's end; the pilgrim castles that stood two hundred years are emptied to the tide. Molay lives through the extinction of Outremer itself: not one stone of the Kingdom of Jerusalem left in Christian hands on the mainland.

stops.name: Limassol, the Temple's headquarters in exile
stops.campa: The remnant of the Order gathers at Limassol on Cyprus, the new head of a house without a homeland. The white banner still flies, but over a garrison island, not a kingdom. In the chapter that follows, Molay speaks for reform: discipline restored, the treasury husbanded, the eyes of the brethren kept fixed on the coast they have lost. The Grand Master Thibaud Gaudin, who carried the Order's treasure out of Acre, does not long survive. The brethren look to the hard veteran of the Franche-Comté.

stops.name: Limassol, elected Grand Master of the Temple
stops.campa: Sometime before the twentieth of April, the chapter elects Jacques de Molay the twenty-third and last Grand Master of the Poor Knights of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon. He takes up an office three centuries deep: the seal of the two knights on one horse, the beauceant banner, the obedience of thousands from Cyprus to the Atlantic. His charge is plain and, as it will prove, impossible: to hold the Order together and win back the Holy Land. He will spend the rest of his life at both, and be granted neither.

stops.name: Nicosia, the Temple against the King of Cyprus
stops.campa: In the little kingdom that is now his whole ground, Molay guards the Order's liberties against the Lusignan crown. King Henry II would bind the great orders to his will; the Grand Master, back from the West, defends the Temple's privileges as jealously as he defends the coast. When the crown itself is torn between Henry and his brother Amaury of Tyre, the Templars stand with Amaury, who seizes power and sends the king into exile. It is a hard, worldly stewardship: an order of warrior-monks entangled in the feuds of a Frankish island, keeping its strength intact for the reconquest still dreamed of.

stops.name: Famagusta, the fleet sails to raid the Syrian coast
stops.campa: From Famagusta sixteen galleys stand out to sea under Admiral Baudouin de Picquigny, Templars and Hospitallers and the men of Cyprus aboard. They fall upon the Egyptian and Syrian shore: Rosetta, Alexandria, the wreck of Acre, Tortosa, Maraclea, burning and taking spoil, holding nothing. It is a raid, not a return, and Molay knows it. But word runs through Christendom that the Mongol Ilkhan Ghazan will come down from the north against the Mamluk, and the Grand Master stakes the Order's strength on the hope of that alliance from the East.

stops.name: Tortosa, the raid on the mainland, the Mongol who never comes
stops.campa: The great design of Molay's grand-mastership hangs on the Mongols of Persia. If Ghazan the Ilkhan comes down through Syria against the Mamluk, the Cypriot host and the military orders will land on the coast and take Tortosa, and the Holy Land is opened again. An ambassador of Ghazan sails with the raiders; the Grand Master lands men on the Syrian shore and waits. But the Mongols come late or not at all, turned back, beaten at Homs and at Shaqhab south of Damascus. The Franks hold the beach a season and re-embark. The alliance from the East, prayed for through years, dissolves like a mirage.
